blocks.h: Why binary search on the speed?
p: If a speed `s` finishes in time, any faster speed does too, so feasibility is monotone: False…False True…True. Binary search finds the smallest True using O(log max) feasibility checks, each O(n).
`ceil(p / mid)` uses floating division; for huge piles integer arithmetic `(p + mid - 1) // mid` is safer because it avoids rounding error.

875.takeaway: Koko bananas: binary search the eating speed with a monotone 'finishes in h hours?' check.

head: Code
Meaning

The node and its whole right subtree are above the range
The node is inside the range; both sides may hold more values

p: The in-range values are 10, 7 and 15, which sum to 32. The nodes 5 and 18 are out of range, and the subtrees below them that cannot contain in-range values are skipped.

In a BST everything left of a node is smaller and everything right of it is larger. If `root.val < low`, every value in its left subtree is also `< low`, so only the right side can contain anything in range. The reverse holds for `root.val > high`. A plain DFS (Depth-First Search) that visits every node would be O(n); pruning gives O(h + k) for k values in range.

bullets: Time: O(n) worst case, O(h + k) typically with pruning.

938.takeaway: Range sum in a BST: prune whole subtrees that cannot overlap [low, high] using the BST ordering.

blocks.h: Why put cameras on parents of leaves?
p: A camera covers its node, its parent and its children. A leaf's camera covers only the leaf and its parent, while a camera on the leaf's parent covers the parent, the leaf (and its sibling) and the grandparent. So placing cameras on leaves' parents dominates placing them on leaves, and the bottom-up greedy repeats that argument at every level.

968.takeaway: Binary tree cameras: bottom-up greedy with three states (uncovered, has camera, covered); put a camera on the parent of any uncovered child.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix sum modulo k, kept small and non-negative (Python's `%` returns a non-negative result for positive k, even when the sum is negative)
How many earlier prefixes (including the empty one) had remainder `s`
So subarrays that start at index 0 are counted
Each earlier prefix with the SAME remainder gives a subarray whose sum is divisible by k
Two prefixes with equal remainders differ by a multiple of k
Record the current prefix after counting
A prefix must not pair with itself

blocks.h: Why equal remainders mean divisible sums
p: `sum(i..j) = prefix[j] − prefix[i−1]`. If both prefixes leave the same remainder mod k, their difference is a multiple of k. So the answer is the number of pairs of equal remainders: a hash map counts them in one pass.

In C++/Java `-3 % 5` is `-3`, so you must add k before taking the modulus again. Python's `%` already returns a non-negative result, so this code needs no fix; in other languages normalise with `((s % k) + k) % k`.

974.takeaway: Subarray sums divisible by k: count equal prefix-sum remainders with a hash map; normalise negatives.
